query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy (HEA), degradation at 700–900 °C in either oxidizing (air) or reducing (5 % H₂/N₂) atmospheres is governed by Ti- and Al-enriched nano-segregated cell/column boundaries inherited from the rapid solidification of laser-powder-bed fusion (LPBF). These boundary regions act as fast-diffusion short-circuit paths and chemical hot-spots: (1) in air they undergo preferential TiO₂ ± Al₂O₃ formation that remains discontinuous and porous, enabling continued inward O diffusion and breakaway oxidation; (2) in H₂-containing gas they promote hydrogen ingress and Ti-hydride/TiC formation, causing boundary embrittlement. Homogenizing heat treatment that dissolves the segregation prior to exposure will eliminate these fast paths, reduce selective oxidation/hydrogen uptake, and thereby retard mass-gain and mechanical property loss.
generation.material_initial_state: As-built LPBF Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy with single-phase fcc matrix containing nano-scale Ti–Al-rich segregation/precipitates along cellular and interdendritic boundaries.
generation.intervention: Solutionizing (homogenization) at 1150 °C for 2 h followed by water quench to produce a chemically homogeneous fcc solid solution with segregation and precipitates dissolved.
generation.conditions: Isothermal exposure for 100 h at 800 °C in (a) flowing dry air (~21 % O₂) and (b) flowing 5 % H₂ / N₂ (reducing).
generation.structural_mediator: Ti–Al-enriched cellular boundary regions (L1₂/B2 nano-clusters) that provide short-circuit diffusion paths and local reservoirs of highly reactive Ti and Al.
generation.mechanism:
1. Oxidizing gas: Rapid outward diffusion of Ti and Al through boundary paths leads to non-protective TiO₂±Al₂O₃ nodules; Cr is locally depleted, preventing formation of a continuous Cr₂O₃ or Al₂O₃ scale and causing accelerated, non-parabolic oxidation.
2. Reducing gas: The same boundaries facilitate inward hydrogen diffusion; Ti reacts to form brittle TiHₓ (and/or TiC if C is available), promoting boundary decohesion and loss of ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome:
Relative to the as-built baseline, the homogenized material will show:
• ≤40 % of the mass gain in air and ≤50 % of the hydrogen uptake in H₂/N₂.
• Shallower external oxide scales (≤2 µm vs 5–10 µm) and reduced internal oxidation depth.
• Retention of >80 % of room-temperature tensile ductility after exposure, whereas as-built samples retain <40 %.
• Absence (or >90 % reduction) of Ti-rich oxides/hydrides at prior cell boundaries in cross-section.
generation.baseline: As-built LPBF material exposed under identical atmospheres and times without prior homogenization, exhibiting its current (literature-reported) oxidation/hydrogen-embrittlement behavior.
generation.boundary: Temperatures 700–900 °C; exposures ≤200 h; gases limited to dry air or mildly reducing 5 % H₂/N₂. Outside these ranges (e.g., >1000 °C, water-vapor-rich or halogenated atmospheres), additional mechanisms (e.g., volatile CrOₓ formation, halide fluxing) may dominate and the hypothesis may no longer hold.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative magnitudes (exact mass-gain factors, oxide continuity threshold) are approximate because no prior oxidation data for this specific AM HEA exist. The relative importance of Ti vs Al reactivity and possible Cr volatilization remain to be resolved.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of coupons: (i) as-built LPBF and (ii) homogenized (1150 °C/2 h/water-quench). Expose both sets at 800 °C for 100 h in (a) dry air and (b) 5 % H₂/N₂. After exposure, perform: (1) mass-change measurement (TGA or weight gain), (2) cross-sectional SEM/EDS mapping for oxide/hydride distribution, (3) TEM to detect boundary oxides/hydrides, (4) glow-discharge or melt extraction for hydrogen content, (5) room-temperature tensile tests for residual ductility.
measurements: Elemental maps of Ti, Al, O, H
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the homogenized samples show (i) mass gain or hydrogen uptake within ±10 % of the as-built samples, AND (ii) comparable oxide/hydride morphology and depth, OR (iii) similar post-exposure ductility loss (<10 % difference), then the hypothesis that boundary segregation controls degradation is falsified.
